4. The aforesaid cases of the respondents were contested by the petitioner Company by filing separate written statements denying the material allegations and stating inter alia that the respondents were not employees or worker in their establishment. It was further stated that the said respondents were in fact employees of M/s. Nawab and Company Security Service (NCSS) as Security Guards and were in their pay roll and that the petitioner Company did not pay their pay their wages directly to them or maintain their employment records. It was also denied that the petitioner Company gave any assurance to the said respondent that their employment would be confirmed by making permanent employee after 3 month of their service as alleged by them. It has been further stated that the grievance petition dated 11.10.2000 sent by the said respondent was found misconceived by the petitioner Company and accordingly rejected by their letter dated. 6.12.2000. 

 7. In Writ petition. No. 884 of 2001 the respondent No. 2 and 3 and in Writ petition No.885 of 2001 the respondent No. 2 are contesting the Rules by filing Affidavits-in-opposition denying all the material allegations and contending inter alia that they are working as Security Guards under the petitioner's establishment but the petitioner Company is trying to treat them as workers of one Nawab and Co. which has got no footing. It is further stated that the petitioner company is a multi national company and they were verbally employed by Mr. Tarashima, Business Manager of Chiyoda Corporation and they are performing their duties in the petitioner Establishment. It is further asserted that the said Tarachirna told the said .respondents that he would issue their written appointment letter within a short time but ultimately did not do so. 

 8. Mr. Momammod Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the said respondents failed to prove that they were workers of the petitioner Company by exhibiting any documents. The learned Advocate has drawn our attention to the judgment and order dated  20.12.2000 passed in payment of wages Case (Annexure F to the Writ petition) where the Labour Court presided by the same Judge held that the said Respondent were in the employment of Nawab and Co's Security Services who had the duty to pay wages' .bonus etc. to them and directed the said Nawab and Co. to pay the Respondent No.2 all arrear wages and benefits, if any as may be due to them and accordingly sub miss that the said respondents are employees/ workers of the said Nawab and Co. The learned Advocate further submits that the complaint cases filed in the Labour Court are not maintainable under section 25 (I) (h) of the said Act since no prior grievance petition within the meaning of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 was proved. In this respect he relies upon the judgment delivered in the case of M/S. Adamjee Jute Mills Limited Vs. Chairman, Labour Court and others reported in 42 DLR (1990) 275. The learned Advocate next also submits that the impugned judgment suffers from legal infirmities since it was not based on any evidence. 

 14. Finally from the impugned judgment it appears that the Labour Court took into consideration that the second party in its written statement stated that Ms. Nawab & Company was engaged "to supply" security personal for the petitioner company and that the said court took the view that the word "engage" means to arrange to employ or hire somebody for some purposes and as such the court came to the finding -that the petitioner company hired the respondent through M/s Nawab & Company for their service in the petitioner company. In our opinion the Labour Court should not have taken such simplistic view and come to a conclusion as to whether the said Respondents were the employees of the petitioner company or some one else without considering the details of evidence specially when the matter was in dispute between the parties. The respondents could well have been engaged by the said NCS not only for working for NCSs but also for another third party as well as for the petitioner's Establishment. What matters is the terms and conditions of their employment and not simply the use of the word 'engage' Thus in our opinion the Labour Court appears to have come to its conclusion by mere surmises and conjectures.
